scope: All 20 original lead source-first findings for chunk 15 compared individually with actual draft parent meanings and stance and the already item-reviewed component proposals. This is source-first reconciliation, not a new full-record or repaired-value approval.

rows.source_first_requirement: United Irishmen sought independence and organized through rural Defenders, whose grievances were more local and sectarian. French strategy needed proof of a rising while Irish leaders awaited intervention. Repression, arrests and uneven outbreaks preceded late French landings.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The intervention and rebellion parents preserve different Irish groups and aims. Retain the mutual-waiting problem, local Defenders’ grievances, state pre-emption and separate 1796/1798 episodes; recent full-page rereads 341–343 confirm the distinctions.

rows.source_first_requirement: Wexford, Vinegar Hill, Humbert’s Mayo landing and Ballinamuck were separate episodes. Doyle emphasizes limited reach, inadequate French commitment and large death toll, while distinguishing comparison with Warsaw and French Terror.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Separate rebellion and expedition treatments retain Wexford/Vinegar Hill, late Humbert landing and Ballinamuck. Preserve geographic limits, inadequate French commitment and exact comparative death-toll denominators; Tone did not arrive in Humbert’s own expedition.

rows.source_first_requirement: Initial Dutch sympathy and representative traditions mattered. Federalist-unitary stalemate, rejected 1797 draft, French-backed January purge and democratic 1798 constitution preceded attempted self-perpetuation and Daendels’s June coup, followed by regular elections.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Two Batavian parents preserve constitution and interventions. Final records must distinguish January purge, democratic constitutional design, self-perpetuation and June removal followed by elections. Preserve the newly noted 344 two-years chronology wording rather than silently normalizing it.

rows.source_first_requirement: Occupation costs, British war and blockade, colonial loss, French tariffs and disrupted charity impoverished cities. Orange restoration and neutrality offered no easy alternatives; some domestic autonomy persisted despite French interference.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Economic, invasion and comparative parents provide routes. Keep occupation costs, commercial exclusion and disestablishment’s welfare effects explicit, alongside constrained alternatives and meaningful domestic autonomy. Neither all Dutch sympathy nor all independence vanished immediately.

rows.source_first_requirement: Rendered whole page: map caption identifies territorial expansion, with visually distinct annexation, French occupation and sister-republic categories. Graph/map internals are excluded by policy, so this inspection does not generate subject evidence from internal labels.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The eligible caption identifies expansion as the topic; internal shading, categories, labels and keys are excluded. Apply source-scope-disposition.v3 and its exact rendered caption binding. The source-first visual description is not authority to create internal-map evidence or mandatory geographic distinctions.

rows.source_first_requirement: Successive occupations treated Belgium as an extractive war resource; departmentalization and annexation ended extraordinary requisitions but introduced French laws. Rural hostility contrasts with urban accommodation and later industrial opportunity in the French market.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Occupation/annexation and social-response parents preserve Belgian phases. Retain extraordinary requisitions ending with incorporation, subsequent French laws, urban economic opportunity and persistent rural hostility; pragmatism does not establish French identity.

rows.source_first_requirement: Clerical confiscation, oath refusal and conscription escalated into 1798 rural uprising. Rebels had local/religious aims and limited urban or elite support; French repression was more bloody. Passive resistance continued and recruitment remained low.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Religious-policy and revolt parents provide distinct routes. Preserve conscription as trigger, local religious goals, weak elite/urban support, severe repression and continuing evasion. Separate laws ordering deportation from numbers actually seized or transported.

rows.source_first_requirement: Natural-frontier claims conflicted with peace strategy and German territorial interests. Hoche’s proposed Cis-Rhenan client state, Reubell’s annexation policy, provisional international consent and administrative departments had different statuses and dates.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The Rhineland and diplomatic parents preserve the proposed Cis-Rhenan alternative, Reubell’s preference, administrative assimilation and delayed legal settlement. Do not label a proposal an existing republic or infer all exploitation began only after formal annexation.

rows.source_first_requirement: Repeated occupation impoverished a front-line region. Customs severed Rhine commerce; flight of prince-bishops wrecked court-service economies. Feudal dues/tithes were retained for revenue before abolition; rental substitution diluted relief. Clerical resistance lacked a mass uprising amid dense troops and absence of conscription.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Economic and religious parents retain distinct mechanisms. Preserve customs disruption, lost court demand, temporary retention of dues/tithes for revenue and rental substitution, plus dense occupation and absent conscription explaining passive rather than mass armed resistance.

rows.source_first_requirement: Italian conquests made Swiss Alpine passes strategically important. Ochs and La Harpe sought reform/emancipation, but local revolts pursued diverse older aims. France shifted from several states to one imposed constitution, coercing reluctant cantons.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The Helvetic parent and comparative record preserve strategic passes, reform advocates and imposed unity. Retain Ochs/La Harpe, distinct Vaud and other local aims, changed French plans and absence of a convention; centralization cannot stand for local democratic consent.

rows.source_first_requirement: City treasuries financed French armies and Egypt. Conscription demands met legislative refusal; rationalizing reform was unevenly received. Catholic valleys resisted both religion policy and loss of established democratic autonomy; wartime requisitions defeated promises of restraint.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The occupation parent preserves both reform and resistance. Keep treasury transfers including Egypt finance, refusal of manpower demands and Catholic valleys’ existing democratic autonomy, with wartime requisitions undermining restraint. Opposition to centralization was not opposition to democracy as such.

rows.source_first_requirement: No general republicanization plan initially governed the invasion; Alba patriots were abandoned. Educated urban radicals hoped to revive Enlightenment reform after reaction, but French leaders suspected Year II politics and weak popular support, aiming first at strategic gains and extraction.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The Italian patriot and Bonaparte parents preserve improvised policy and limited social reach. Retain Alba’s abandonment, educated urban reform hopes, French fear of Year II radicalism and priority of extraction; no settled initial plan for general republicanization or national unity is supported.

rows.source_first_requirement: War contributions, requisitions, treasury and pawnshop seizures, art removal and generals’ profits funded armies and France. Pavia’s revolt and sack exemplify resistance; many dispersed rural revolts combined religious outrage and material loss.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The exploitation and revolt parents provide routes. Preserve pawnshop/treasury seizures and welfare effects alongside art removal, army finance and generals’ gains. Pavia and dispersed rural resistance do not constitute one unified nationalist movement.

rows.source_first_requirement: Bonaparte encouraged limited cooperation while suppressing Milanese unity demands. Conservative Cispadane election results and strategic frontier problems helped produce Cisalpine consolidation. Venice became compensation for Austria; the new constitution and first officers were imposed.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Formation, unity and Venice parents preserve contingencies. Retain the conservative Cispadane result, strategic boundaries, imposed Cisalpine constitution/officers and Venetian bargaining. Correct the internally inconsistent earlier Cispadane date through explicit source uncertainty rather than unmarked normalization.

rows.source_first_requirement: France demanded troop maintenance, its own army and commercial preferences. Treaty resistance prompted a purge; later conflicts over radicalism, constitutional restriction and Brune’s disobedience caused repeated reversals. Jacobin refugees continued to seek Italian unity.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The Cisalpine parent must retain exact successive military/trade demands, treaty resistance and purges, including Brune’s disobedience and reversals. Apply the added reviewer’s correction that post-departure obligations were not personally imposed by absent Bonaparte; do not substitute generic French control for the sequence.

rows.source_first_requirement: Ligurian constitution was locally drafted and plebiscitary but financial refusal provoked a coup. Rome’s imposed institutions used antique labels while allowing French command to legislate; religious/economic changes undermined charity and popular support.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Distinct Ligurian and Roman parents preserve local drafting/plebiscite versus imposed antique-named institutions under French command. Retain coercive fiscal limits and Roman charity/religious-economic disruption; names do not establish ancient institutional identity.

rows.source_first_requirement: Championnet’s intervention exceeded Directory wishes and faced lazzaroni resistance. Retreat exposed Jacobins to Ruffo’s Holy Faith army; Ruffo mobilized social, rural-urban and religious grievances, even offering feudal relief before reformers. Subsequent reprisals were demanded over his opposition.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The Parthenopean and Sanfedist parents preserve Championnet exceeding policy, lazzaroni opposition, withdrawal and Ruffo’s mixed mobilization. Preserve his early feudal relief and opposition to the restored court’s reprisals; restoration forces were not a uniform command or programme.

rows.source_first_requirement: French pressure displaced Piedmont’s king and annexation was rigged; Tuscany was occupied for wartime resources. Resistance drew on older anti-reform and subsistence grievances and included anti-Jewish attacks.
rows.independent_reconciliation: Piedmont, Tuscany and revolt parents retain distinct routes, royal displacement, manipulated annexation and resource motives. Preserve urban as well as rural hardship, older Tuscan disputes and anti-Jewish violence; maintain the 366 chronology discrepancy explicitly.

rows.source_first_requirement: Peasants linked foreign soldiers, exactions, impiety and urban collaborators; some Jacobins also opposed French control. Langhe peasants carried Jacobin martyr images in an anti-annexation rising, complicating ideological labels.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The resistance and patriot parents preserve divergent antagonisms. Keep Langhe use of Jacobin martyr images and Jacobin opposition to French domination as explicit complications; symbols alone do not prove allegiance to French occupation or a single reactionary coalition.

rows.source_first_requirement: Local opposition magnified coalition pressure. Stockach and Suvorov’s advances exposed overstretch and collapsed sister republics. Bonaparte learned late of European losses and left his army before receiving evacuation orders; eventual surrender followed.
rows.independent_reconciliation: The military-collapse and departure parents preserve interaction between coalition armies and local resistance. Apply exact battle/defeat sequence repairs, keep Bonaparte’s information and departure before receipt of evacuation orders, and distinguish eventual Egyptian surrender from his personal escape.
